Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Samuel is a 72-year-old retired Coast Guard veteran who lives with his wife, Dorothy, in a quiet suburban home. For decades, he managed to push forward, but the memory of the toxic chemical exposure he endured during a response operation has never truly left him. It happened aboard a cargo vessel anchored off the coast, where a ruptured container had released an oily, acrid vapor into the hold. He remembers the moment with photographic clarity: the way the afternoon light caught the drifting haze, the silence that fell after the emergency klaxon cut off, and the sudden realization that the air itself had become something to fear. That silence—the unnatural stillness before the alarm was silenced, before the crew held their breath—still haunts him. Even now, inside his own home, a stretch of quiet in the living room or a pause in Dorothy’s voice makes his chest tighten. He has come to believe that silence is a warning, a precursor to something dangerous. He finds himself scanning the room, checking the windows, listening for the wrong kind of quiet.

The memories themselves are overwhelming. When they surface—and they do, without warning—they play like a film he cannot stop. He sees the same sequence: the deck, the haze, the faces of his shipmates, the scrambled evacuation. The emotional force of it hits him so hard he has to stop whatever he is doing, sometimes gripping the kitchen counter until his knuckles whiten. The vividness is unsettling; it is as if he is looking at snapshots held inches from his eyes, each detail still crisp decades later. He has tried for years not to think about it, because he is certain that if he lets himself dwell on the event, he will not be able to handle it. He believes he cannot cope with even the smallest upset anymore—a broken coffee maker or a missed appointment can leave him irritable and shaky, confirming his fear that his resilience is gone.

The world, to Samuel, feels fundamentally unsafe. He carries that alertness with him everywhere, but it is most constant at home, the one place where a person should feel at ease. Instead, he finds himself on guard, double-checking the locks, listening for footsteps, interpreting a neighbor’s car door as a possible threat. The physical reactions come without his permission: a sudden bang from the garage makes his heart pound and his palms sweat; the smell of cleaning solvents, even diluted, makes his stomach turn. He avoids passing the hardware store where they sell industrial chemicals, and he has stopped reading news stories about environmental disasters. His wife notices that he flinches when she walks up behind him, and that he rarely sits with his back to the room. She has tried to ask about his service, but he waves her off, repeating that he does not want to talk about it. He knows that if he starts, he might not stop, and he is terrified of what that would unleash.

Over the months and years, these habits have carved a distance between them. Samuel spends long hours in his workshop, where the hum of a fan drowns out the quiet, or in front of the television, volume turned up. He has stopped attending the Coast Guard retiree gatherings he once enjoyed, because the stories of others bring his own memory too close. His world has grown smaller. It was only last month, when a prolonged silence in the house—Dorothy had gone to the store, and the furnace had cycled off—triggered a full panic attack, that she insisted he seek help. Now, sitting in the therapist’s office, Samuel shifts in his chair, wary of what will come next. He is afraid that talking will break something inside him, but beneath that fear is a quiet hope: that he might finally find a way to sit in silence without feeling that it is a threat.
